display_title_he: סימון מים של OpenAI באיחוד האירופי
short_summary: OpenAI is introducing invisible text watermarking for ChatGPT and Codex in the European Union to comply with regional AI regulations.

sources.name: TechCrunch
sources.title: OpenAI will start watermarking ChatGPT’s text in the EU

sources.name: The Verge
sources.title: OpenAI is adding text watermarking in ChatGPT and Codex

paragraphs: OpenAI has officially announced that it will begin integrating an invisible watermark into text generated by ChatGPT and Codex within the European Union. According to the company, this implementation is specifically designed to comply with the strict transparency mandates established by the EU AI Act, which officially took effect on August 2. These regulatory rules require artificial intelligence corporations to mark machine-generated content in a manner that allows other technological systems to easily identify it.

Over the coming weeks, the new watermark will gradually roll out to eligible ChatGPT and Codex users across all subscription plans, but availability will remain strictly restricted to the European Union for now. OpenAI stated that it is not deploying text watermarking as a global default at launch, choosing instead a regional approach to learn from real-world use and feedback. Concurrently, developers utilizing OpenAI's API anywhere across the world can choose to opt in and enable the feature for select models, though it remains deactivated by default. OpenAI is also working with cloud partners to make watermarking available for model outputs accessed through their services in the coming weeks.

The underlying watermarking method, detailed in a technical report called textGrain and co-written with researchers from the University of Pennsylvania and Yale, relies on a secret key to sort next-word predictions. Rather than attaching a visible symbol, the system subtly shapes the model's word choices to generate an imperceptible pattern that specialized detectors can recognize using only the text and the key. Because this pattern resides directly within the vocabulary itself, it travels alongside the text whenever it is copied and pasted. OpenAI noted that the watermark does not identify individual users or reveal their prompts and conversations, and it causes no meaningful degradation in model performance.

Nevertheless, the technology faces several recognized limitations. OpenAI's internal testing indicates that replacing ten percent of the words with synonyms can drop detection rates from about ninety-two percent down to sixty-six percent. Furthermore, short passages, mathematical answers, and translated texts are considerably more difficult to identify accurately. Because of these challenges, along with the risk of missed watermarks and false positives, initial detector access is being granted exclusively to approved researchers and expert organizations on a case-by-case basis rather than to the general public.

This development follows a similar decision made two months prior by competitor Anthropic, which announced worldwide text watermarking for its Claude assistant to meet EU requirements, a move that drew backlash from some users who argued they supplied the instructions while the AI was merely a tool. While major tech firms including Anthropic, Google, Meta, Microsoft, and OpenAI have committed to following the EU code of practice, text watermarking continues to provoke debate regarding authorship, editing, and the boundaries of user contribution. Previously, OpenAI had built a text watermark but held off on releasing it partly over concerns that users might switch to rival companies that did not use watermarking.

facts.fact: OpenAI announced it will start adding an invisible watermark to text generated by ChatGPT and Codex in the European Union.
The move complies with the transparency rules of the EU AI Act, which took effect on August 2.
The watermark is rolling out over the coming weeks to eligible users on all plans in the EU only, and will not be a global default at launch.
Developers using OpenAI's API globally can opt in for select models starting Monday.
The method, called textGrain, subtly shapes word choices to leave an invisible pattern for detectors while preserving model performance.
OpenAI published a technical report co-written with researchers from the University of Pennsylvania and Yale.

Initial detector access is restricted to approved researchers and expert organizations to evaluate reliability.
Anthropic previously announced watermarking for Claude in August to meet EU requirements, drawing some user backlash.
